issues.legal_issue: Findings of bona fide personal need may be upheld where the courts have made clear factual findings from the evidence, notwithstanding an inadequately detailed pleading.
material_facts: The eviction suit alleged that the landlords required the premises for their bona fide personal use.
The trial court dismissed the suit on personal-need grounds, but the first appellate court reversed that finding and decreed eviction.
The first appellate court and the High Court made clear findings on personal need after assessing the evidence adduced by both sides.
The tenants presented evidence that the landlords had other shops, but the courts found their evidence too meagre.
The Supreme Court held that the pleading defect did not justify disregarding the evidence on personal need.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to uphold the first appellate court’s findings on bona fide personal need; the pleading defect did not require the evidence to be ignored.
issues.legal_principle: In an eviction suit based on bona fide personal necessity following termination of tenancy under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, a defect in the detail of the pleadings does not warrant obliterating evidence adduced on the issue if the courts have assessed that evidence and recorded the requisite factual findings. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

rule.if: eviction_appeal_on_personal_need and appellate_findings_based_on_evidence and evidence_adduced_on_both_sides and contrary_evidence_found_meagre

predicates.eviction_appeal_on_personal_need: The proceeding is an appeal in an eviction suit in which bona fide personal need is in issue.
predicates.appellate_findings_based_on_evidence: The appellate courts assess the evidence and record factual findings on the alleged personal need.
predicates.evidence_adduced_on_both_sides: Both the party asserting personal need and the opposing party present evidence on that issue.
predicates.contrary_evidence_found_meagre: The courts find the opposing party’s evidence on the alleged need too meagre to displace the evidence supporting it.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal concerns personal need and the appellate courts assess evidence from both sides, findings based on that evidence stand despite a pleading defect where the opposing evidence is found meagre.

issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court need not admit additional evidence or remand an eviction case when no request for additional evidence was made in the first appeal and the circumstances do not justify further evidence.
material_facts: The tenants applied under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for permission to adduce additional evidence in the High Court during the second appeal.
They had made no such request before the first appellate court.
The evidence they had already adduced on the landlords’ alleged lack of personal need was found too meagre.
The High Court did not permit additional evidence, and the Supreme Court found no justification for a remand.
issues.conclusion: The High Court committed no error by refusing additional evidence at the second appellate stage, and there was no justification for remanding the case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the application under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the circumstances of this case and concluded that additional evidence was not warranted at the second appellate stage, particularly when it had not been sought in the first appeal. It relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

rule.if: second_appeal_in_eviction_case and additional_evidence_requested_in_second_appeal and not additional_evidence_requested_in_first_appeal and existing_opposing_evidence_found_meagre

predicates.second_appeal_in_eviction_case: The proceeding is a second appeal arising from an eviction suit.
predicates.additional_evidence_requested_in_second_: A party asks the second appellate court to permit additional evidence.
predicates.additional_evidence_requested_in_first_a: A party asked the first appellate court to permit additional evidence.
predicates.existing_opposing_evidence_found_meagre: The evidence already presented against the asserted personal need is found too meagre.

issues.definition: In a second appeal in an eviction case, refusal of additional evidence and remand is justified when the request is made only at that stage and the existing opposing evidence is meagre.

issues.legal_issue: A request to revoke special leave need not be examined after the Court has already directed that the appeal proceed to an early hearing instead of revoking leave.
material_facts: The respondents asked the Supreme Court to revoke the special leave.
An earlier order of the Court had directed that the appeal be posted for an early hearing rather than revoking the special leave.
The Court declined to examine the request for revocation.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not examine the request to revoke special leave.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on its earlier order directing an early hearing instead of revocation and did not state a further legal rule or rely on any earlier case.

predicates.appeal_by_special_leave: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.revocation_requested: A party asks the Court to revoke the special leave.
predicates.earlier_order_directed_early_hearing_ins: The Court previously directed the appeal to be heard early instead of revoking the special leave.

issues.definition: When special leave is challenged after the Court has directed an early hearing instead of revocation, the Court may leave the revocation request unexamined.
